title: Indicators
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB08#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB08#N.3a, AB08#N.7a, AB08#N.8, AB08#N.10a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: End point
items.clue: The stage of a titration at which the indicator visibly changes.

items.label: Phenolphthalein
items.clue: A weak acid, HInd, whose Ind⁻ form is pink; it changes at about pH 8–10.

items.label: Equivalence point
items.clue: The stage at which acid and base have reacted in the stoichiometric ratio.

items.label: Universal indicator
items.clue: A mixture of several weak acids with different pKa values, used to estimate pH.

questions.stem: An indicator, HInd, has pKa = 3.7: HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq). HInd is red and Ind⁻ is yellow. What colour does the indicator show in a solution of pH 6.0, and why?

options.text: Yellow, as Ind⁻ predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Red, as the solution is acidic, with its pH below 7.
Red, as HInd predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Orange, as HInd and Ind⁻ are equal at equilibrium.

questions.explanation: At pH 6.0, [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, far below Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁴, so the equilibrium lies to the right: [Ind⁻]/[HInd] ≈ 200. The colour is yellow.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three indicators are available, with these pH ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0. Which choice of indicator, with its reason, is correct?

options.text: Phenolphthalein, as the salt CH₃COONa makes the equivalence pH above 7.
Methyl orange, as its range is close to the pKa of ethanoic acid.
Bromothymol blue, as the equivalence point of a titration is at pH 7.
Any of the three, as the pH passes through every range near equivalence.

questions.explanation: At equivalence the flask holds sodium ethanoate; CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes it basic (about pH 8.7). Phenolphthalein's range lies within the steep section.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ammonia is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Which indicator is the most suitable? Ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0; thymol blue 8.0–9.6; alizarin yellow 10.1–12.0.
questions.explanation: Strong acid + weak base: NH₄⁺ makes the equivalence point acidic (about pH 5.3), and the steep section runs down to about pH 3.5. Methyl orange changes there.

questions.stem: Methyl orange can be written HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq), with HInd red and Ind⁻ yellow. A few drops are added to aqueous ammonia: the solution is yellow. Hydrochloric acid is run in. Near the end it turns orange, then red. Why?

options.text: Added H⁺ shifts the indicator equilibrium to the right, so the red Ind⁻ form builds up.
Once the ammonia is used up, added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium left, so red HInd builds up.
The indicator reacts with the ammonium chloride formed, making a red salt.
The solution turns red at exactly pH 7, when the ammonia is neutralised.

questions.explanation: While NH₃ remains, it mops up the H⁺. Past equivalence [H⁺] jumps, the pH falls through methyl orange's range, and [HInd]/[Ind⁻] = [H⁺]/Ka becomes large.
